title: The mind's own country
hook: to his mother: wherever I go, the sky and my mind come with me (Consolation to Helvia 8)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the flattering letter from Corsica. Your line was even seneca. Did you catch a flattery, and say something plain instead? Day five hundred sixteen.

Same island. Same exile. Same man. But a different letter. Before or after the one we read yesterday, nobody is sure which, Seneca wrote from Corsica to his mother, Helvia. Think about how strange that is. Usually the person in trouble receives comfort. Here the exile is the one comforting. His mother had lost her husband, and now her son was gone too, to a rocky island across the sea. So Seneca wrote to tell her he was all right, and why. Today: the mind's own country.
screen: `SAME ISLAND, DIFFERENT LETTER.` → `THE EXILE COMFORTS HIS MOTHER.` → `THE MIND'S OWN COUNTRY.`

segments.voice: First, a son consoles his mother. Seneca knows the genre: a consolation is usually written to the one grieving by someone safe at home. He says he's doing something new, writing as the one she's grieving for. Second, people have always moved. He reminds her how much of humanity lives far from where it was born: Greeks on the coasts of Italy, Romans in every province. Even Corsica, he says, has changed hands and peoples again and again. Being away from home isn't a strange fate. It's one of the most ordinary human things. Third, two things come along. Seneca quotes two Romans. The scholar Varro said that wherever we go, we have the same nature around us. Brutus said exiles may carry their own virtues with them. Seneca puts them together: the world itself, and your own character, go with you everywhere. No one can exile you from either. Fourth, the sky. In chapter eight he says, roughly, so long as I can look up and see the sun and moon, watch the planets rise and set, and let my mind go out among the heavens, what does it matter what ground I'm standing on? Corsica is small. The sky over it is the same sky that's over Rome. Later in the letter he tells his mother to turn to study, and admits his father wouldn't let her go as far in philosophy as she wanted. It's a tender detail. Exiled, he wants her free too.
screen: `A SON CONSOLES HIS MOTHER.` · `PEOPLE HAVE ALWAYS MOVED.` · `NATURE AND VIRTUE COME ALONG.` · `THE SAME SKY OVER CORSICA.` · then, large: `THE SAME SKY.`

segments.voice: If you can, go to a window, or step outside, and look up. If you can't, picture the sky above wherever you are right now. Day or night, clouds or stars. Breathe slowly, and just look. Then think of someone you love who's far away. Somewhere else, they're under this same sky. Let your mind go out into it for a while, the way Seneca's did on his island. The bell holds the time.
The mind's own country. From exile, Seneca told his mother that the world, his character and the sky came with him wherever he went. Today's word.
Your line: the same sky. Look up at least once today, wherever you're stuck, and remember who else is under it. Day five hundred sixteen.

screen: `DAY 516 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE DEATH IN THE BATH.`

howItsDone: Some people who read the Consolation to Helvia make a habit of looking at the sky when they feel stuck or far from home, as Seneca describes doing on Corsica.

myth: in this letter, Seneca's mother comforts him in exile
it's the other way round: the exile writes to comfort his mother.
Seneca says the world and your own character go with you everywhere
he joins Varro's line and Brutus' line into one.
Seneca says his father encouraged his mother's study of philosophy
he admits his father held her back, and urges her to study now.

fork.setup: you're Seneca, exiled on a rocky island. your mother is grieving for you. what do you write?
options: describe how miserable the island is.
tell her what can't be taken from you, and that the sky is the same.
say nothing, so as not to worry her.
fork.reveal: he wrote to comfort her: nature and character go with us everywhere, and the sky over Corsica is the sky over Rome.

original.note: Latin: the sky, the heavens. What Seneca looked up at from Corsica.

trapdoor: what you thought: think positive when life moves you somewhere you don't want to be.
what it means: two things go with you everywhere, the world and your own character, and no one can exile you from either.
what a scholar hears: Seneca turns the consolatio around, writing as the one being mourned, and quotes Varro and Brutus to make his case.

notes: The order of the Consolations to Polybius and to Helvia is uncertain; 'nobody is sure which' hedged. Confirm.
Helvia had recently lost her husband, Seneca the Elder; confirm the timing relative to the exile.

Ch. 1: Seneca says he is doing something new, consoling as the one mourned. Ch. 6–7: peoples on the move, Corsica's many settlers. Ch. 8: Varro (same nature) and Brutus (virtues go into exile with us); gazing at the heavens. Paraphrased; confirm.
Ch. 17: his father's old-fashioned strictness kept Helvia from fully studying philosophy. Confirm.
